newsitem.title: UK: Russians hope for success on back of Su-37.
newsitem.headline: Russians hope for success on back of Su-37.

text.p: Russian aerospace chiefs, encouraged by huge interest shown in Sukhoi's extraordinary new high-performance Su-37 fighter, on Thursday predicted the country would boost its aircraft sales.

"At ministerial and company level there are hundreds of talks going on which will result in the signing of deals," Russian Defence Industry Minister Zinovy Pak told a news conference at the Farnborough International Air Show.
"I think the progress of military cooperation will be given a boost thanks to the demonstration of the Su-37," he added.

Although a large number of Russian aircraft and helicopters are at Farnborough, all eyes are fixed firmly on the Su-37, which is equipped with moveable engine nozzles which enable it to carry out unprecedented acrobatic feats.
Test pilot Yevgeny Frolov has stunned crowds and competitors with low-speed aerial tricks, including a manoeuvre where the Su-37 carries out a tight loop while remaining stationary in the air.

Sukhoi says the plane can also hang motionless for three to four seconds and will be equipped with both rear- and forward-firing missiles to enable the pilot to engage the enemy whatever his position.

Western experts are divided over whether such feats are useful in modern jet combat but some Russians predict the plane -- now still a prototype -- would make most of the world's fighter aircraft obsolete overnight if introduced.
Sukhoi chief designer Mikhail Simonov was in confident mood, challenging his U.S. competitors to a duel.

"It seems some U.S. pilots say they don't need the Su-37's combat capabilities...We would be happy to stage a dogfight here. If that isn't allowed, we could do it out over the Atlantic," he told a separate news briefing.
"This is very much a soldier's plane. It has to be as reliable as a Kalashnikov automatic rifle and it must be very cheap, while being among the best in its field," he added.

The prospect of increased sales can only cheer up Russia's arms industry, which is recovering slowly from the extensive damage caused by the collapse of the Soviet Union and embargoes against big customers such as the former Yugoslavia and Iraq.
Last year it sold around $7 billion worth of arms, most of it through the state-owned Rosvooruzheniye corporation.

"We are negotiating with other countries at this moment. I can't give you specific details but, as soon as the contracts are signed, you will see Su-37s in other parts of the world," said Rosvooruzheniye chief Ilya Pakholenko.

But large parts of Russia's aviation industry urgently need investment and Pak urged foreign companies not to be shy, saying they should have been encouraged by President Boris Yeltsin's reelection in June.
"The Russian aviation industry will boost its search for partners since the country has proved the stability of the political system," he said.

Other aircraft on show include Tupolev's Tu-214, the long- range version of the company's much-delayed twin-jet Tu-204 airliner, and the new Ilyushin Il-114 twin-prop commuter airliner as well as the four-jet Il-96M passenger plane.
Military helicopter maker Kamov is also out in force with its Ka-50 Black Shark as well as the Ka-29 ship-borne and the Ka-31 low-level radar-carrying craft.
